- Bounding rectangle computation for paths.

- Approximate the area of a path.
- [fit](https://docs.rs/fit/index.html)
- Fit paths into rectangles.
- [hatching](https://docs.rs/hatching/index.html)
- Generate hatching and dotted patterns in a path.
- [hit_](https://docs.rs/hit_test/index.html)- test
- Determine whether a point is inside a path.
- [length](https://docs.rs/length/index.html)
- Approximate path length.
- [math](https://docs.rs/math/index.html)
- f32 version of the lyon_geom types used everywhere. Most other lyon crates reexport them.
- [measure](https://docs.rs/measure/index.html)
- Perform cached measurements and split operations on a path.
- [raycast](https://docs.rs/raycast/index.html)
- Find the first collision between a ray and a path.
- [rect](https://docs.rs/rect/index.html)
- [rounded_](https://docs.rs/rounded_polygon/index.html)- polygon
- [walk](https://docs.rs/walk/index.html)
- Move at a defined speed along a path.
- [winding](https://docs.rs/winding/index.html)

# lyon_algorithms 1.0.20 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/lyon_algorithms/latest

# lyon::algorithms

A collection of various vector path manipulation algorithms.

- Path bounding box
- Path area
- Path length
- Winding numbers of a path at any position
- Hatching a Path
- Path hit testing
- Path ray casting
- walking along a path

`lyon_algorithms` can be used as a standalone crate or as part of [lyon](https://docs.rs/lyon/) via the `lyon::algorithms` module.

---

# lyon_path - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lyon_path/^1.0.19/

## Expand description

Data structures and traits to work with paths (vector graphics).

To build and consume paths, see the [builder](https://docs.rs/builder/index.html) and
[iterator](https://docs.rs/iterator/index.html) modules.

This crate is reexported in [lyon](https://docs.rs/lyon/).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use lyon_path::Path;
use lyon_path::math::{point};
use lyon_path::builder::*;
// Create a builder object to build the path.
let mut builder = Path::builder();
// Build a simple path.
let mut builder = Path::builder();
builder.begin(point(0.0, 0.0));
builder.line_to(point(1.0, 2.0));
builder.line_to(point(2.0, 0.0));
builder.line_to(point(1.0, 1.0));
builder.close();
// Generate the actual path object.
let path = builder.build();
for event in &path {
    println!("{:?}", event);
}
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [builder](https://docs.rs/builder/index.html)
- Path building utilities.
- [commands](https://docs.rs/commands/index.html)
- A generic representation for paths that allow more control over how endpoints and control points are stored.
- [iterator](https://docs.rs/iterator/index.html)
- Tools to iterate over paths.
- [math](https://docs.rs/math/index.html)
- f32 version of the lyon_geom types used everywhere. Most other lyon crates reexport them.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)
- The default path data structure.
- [path_](https://docs.rs/path_buffer/index.html)- buffer
- A container to store multiple paths contiguously.
- [polygon](https://docs.rs/polygon/index.html)
- Specific path types for polygons.
- [traits](https://docs.rs/traits/index.html)
- `lyon_path`traits reexported here for convenience.

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [forward_](https://docs.rs/macro.forward_to_deserialize_any.html)- to_ - deserialize_ - any - `docsrs`
- Helper macro when implementing the `Deserializer`part of a new data format for Serde.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

## Derive Macros[§](https://docs.rs#derives)

- [Deserialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Deserialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/derive.Serialize.html)- `derive`
- Derive macro available if serde is built with `features = ["derive"]`.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# lyon - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lyon/

## Expand description

GPU-based 2D graphics rendering tools in Rust using path tessellation.

[§](https://docs.rs#crates)Crates

This meta-crate (`lyon`) reexports the following sub-crates for convenience:

- [-](https://docs.rs/lyon_tessellation)- **lyon_tessellation**- Path tessellation routines.
- [-](https://docs.rs/lyon_path)- **lyon_path**- Tools to build and iterate over paths.
- [-](https://docs.rs/lyon_algorithms)- **lyon_algorithms**- Various 2d path related algorithms.
- [-](https://docs.rs/lyon_geom)- **lyon_geom**- 2d utilities for cubic and quadratic bézier curves, arcs and more.
- [-](https://docs.rs/lyon_extra)- **lyon_extra**- Additional testing and debugging tools.

Each `lyon_<name>` crate is reexported as a `<name>` module in `lyon`. For example:

Is equivalent to:

[§](https://docs.rs#feature-flags)Feature flags

serialization using serde can be enabled on each crate using the
`serialization` feature flag (disabled by default).

When using the main crate `lyon`, `lyon_extra` dependencies is disabled by default.
It can be added with the feature flags `extra`.

[§](https://docs.rs#additional-documentation-and-links)Additional documentation and links

- [wgpu example](https://github.com/nical/lyon/tree/main/examples/wgpu).
- [wgpu_svg example](https://github.com/nical/lyon/tree/main/examples/wgpu_svg)similar to the first example, can render a very small subset of SVG.
- There is some useful documentation on the project’s [wiki](https://github.com/nical/lyon/wiki).
- The source code is available on the project’s [git repository](https://github.com/nical/lyon).
- Interested in contributing? Pull requests are welcome. If you would like to help but don’t know
what to do specifically, have a look at the [github issues](https://github.com/nical/lyon/issues), some of which are tagged as[easy](https://github.com/nical/lyon/issues?q=is%3Aissue+is%3Aopen+label%3Aeasy).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

[§](https://docs.rs#tessellating-a-rounded-rectangle)Tessellating a rounded rectangle

The `lyon_tessellation` crate provides a collection of tessellation routines
for common shapes such as rectangles and circles. Let’s have a look at how
to obtain the fill tessellation a rectangle with rounded corners:

```
use lyon::math::{Box2D, Point, point};
use lyon::path::{Winding, builder::BorderRadii};
use lyon::tessellation::{FillTessellator, FillOptions, VertexBuffers};
use lyon::tessellation::geometry_builder::simple_builder;
fn main() {
    let mut geometry: VertexBuffers<Point, u16> = VertexBuffers::new();
    let mut geometry_builder = simple_builder(&mut geometry);
    let options = FillOptions::tolerance(0.1);
    let mut tessellator = FillTessellator::new();
    let mut builder = tessellator.builder(
        &options,
        &mut geometry_builder,
    );
    builder.add_rounded_rectangle(
        &Box2D { min: point(0.0, 0.0), max: point(100.0, 50.0) },
        &BorderRadii {
            top_left: 10.0,
            top_right: 5.0,
            bottom_left: 20.0,
            bottom_right: 25.0,
        },
        Winding::Positive,
    );
    builder.build();
    // The tessellated geometry is ready to be uploaded to the GPU.
    println!(" -- {} vertices {} indices",
        geometry.vertices.len(),
        geometry.indices.len()
    );
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#building-and-tessellating-an-arbitrary-path)Building and tessellating an arbitrary path

```
extern crate lyon;
use lyon::math::{point, Point};
use lyon::path::Path;
use lyon::path::builder::*;
use lyon::tessellation::*;
fn main() {
    // Build a Path.
    let mut builder = Path::builder();
    builder.begin(point(0.0, 0.0));
    builder.line_to(point(1.0, 0.0));
    builder.quadratic_bezier_to(point(2.0, 0.0), point(2.0, 1.0));
    builder.cubic_bezier_to(point(1.0, 1.0), point(0.0, 1.0), point(0.0, 0.0));
    builder.close();
    let path = builder.build();
    // Let's use our own custom vertex type instead of the default one.
    #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug)]
    struct MyVertex { position: [f32; 2] };
    // Will contain the result of the tessellation.
    let mut geometry: VertexBuffers<MyVertex, u16> = VertexBuffers::new();
    let mut tessellator = FillTessellator::new();
    {
        // Compute the tessellation.
        tessellator.tessellate_path(
            &path,
            &FillOptions::default(),
            &mut BuffersBuilder::new(&mut geometry, |vertex: FillVertex| {
                MyVertex {
                    position: vertex.position().to_array(),
                }
            }),
        ).unwrap();
    }
    // The tessellated geometry is ready to be uploaded to the GPU.
    println!(" -- {} vertices {} indices",
        geometry.vertices.len(),
        geometry.indices.len()
    );
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#what-is-the-tolerance-variable-in-these-examples)What is the tolerance variable in these examples?

The tessellator operates on flattened paths (that only contains line segments)
so we have to approximate the curves segments with sequences of line segments.
To do so we pick a tolerance threshold which is the maximum distance allowed
between the curve and its approximation.
The documentation of the [lyon_geom](https://docs.rs/lyon_geom) crate provides
more detailed explanations about this tolerance parameter.

[§](https://docs.rs#rendering-the-tessellated-geometry)Rendering the tessellated geometry

Lyon does not provide with any GPU abstraction or rendering backend (for now).
It is up to the user of this crate to decide whether to use OpenGL, vulkan, gfx-rs,
wgpu, glium, or any low level graphics API and how to render it.
The [wgpu example](https://github.com/nical/lyon/tree/main/examples/wgpu)
can be used to get an idea of how to render the geometry (in this case
using wgpu).

# lyon_path - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lyon_path/1.0.19/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lyon_path/index.html

## Expand description

Data structures and traits to work with paths (vector graphics).

To build and consume paths, see the [builder](https://docs.rs/builder/index.html) and
[iterator](https://docs.rs/iterator/index.html) modules.

This crate is reexported in [lyon](https://docs.rs/lyon/).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use lyon_path::Path;
use lyon_path::math::{point};
use lyon_path::builder::*;
// Create a builder object to build the path.
let mut builder = Path::builder();
// Build a simple path.
let mut builder = Path::builder();
builder.begin(point(0.0, 0.0));
builder.line_to(point(1.0, 2.0));
builder.line_to(point(2.0, 0.0));
builder.line_to(point(1.0, 1.0));
builder.close();
// Generate the actual path object.
let path = builder.build();
for event in &path {
    println!("{:?}", event);
}
```

# lyon_geom - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/lyon_geom/1.0.19/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/lyon_geom/index.html

## Expand description

Simple 2D geometric primitives on top of euclid.

This crate is reexported in [lyon](https://docs.rs/lyon/).

[§](https://docs.rs#overview)Overview.

This crate implements some of the maths to work with:

- lines and line segments,
- quadratic and cubic bézier curves,
- elliptic arcs,
- triangles.

[§](https://docs.rs#flattening)Flattening

Flattening is the action of approximating a curve with a succession of line segments.

The tolerance threshold taken as input by the flattening algorithms corresponds to the maximum distance between the curve and its linear approximation. The smaller the tolerance is, the more precise the approximation and the more segments are generated. This value is typically chosen in function of the zoom level.

The figure above shows a close up on a curve (the dotted line) and its linear approximation (the black segments). The tolerance threshold is represented by the light green area and the orange arrow.

`a * x + b * y + c = 0; a * a + b * b = 1`.

- An elliptic arc curve segment using the SVG’s end-point notation.

# moorage 0.0.1 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/moorage/0.0.1

# moorage

Install your self-authored agent **skills and plugins** into one central home, and
wire every agent harness to them from a single source of truth. A small Rust CLI.

*(Renamed from  skilldock, which collided on GitHub.)*

## Commands

```
moorage install   SOURCE [--mode dev|normal] [--skills a,b] [--harnesses claude,pi,omp,codex]
                         [--force] [--dry-run] [--no-post-install]
moorage uninstall NAME... [--dry-run]
moorage update    NAME... [--force] [--dry-run]
moorage list
moorage doctor    [--json]
```
All commands accept the six root overrides (see *Roots* below). `--dry-run` prints the
full action plan — skills, links, hook placements, registration merges, backups,
post_install — and mutates nothing.

## Skills (no manifest — behavior unchanged)

`SOURCE` may be a directory containing `SKILL.md` (single skill) or a repo with
`skills/*/SKILL.md` (multi-skill; scanned one level). The skill **name** comes from
the `SKILL.md` frontmatter `name:` and must be lowercase `[a-z0-9-]`, ≤ 64 chars,
with a non-empty `description:` (pi's discovery rule — enforced so the link name is
correct). A `skills/*` layout is **preferred** over a repo-root `SKILL.md`, so a repo
carrying both installs its `skills/<name>` payloads (the baseline shape).

Each skill installs to `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`:

| Mode | `~/.moorage/skills/{name}`is | Use it when |
|---|---|---|
| `dev`(default) | a symlink to the repo payload | authoring / iterating |
| `normal`(alias:`local`) | a real copy (excludes `.git`,`__pycache__`) | pinned snapshot |

and the agent roots link into the home:

```
~/.agents/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- dev:    repo payload (live)
                           +-->  ~/.moorage/skills/{name} -+
~/.claude/skills/{name}  --+                              +-- normal: a copy in the home
```
oh-my-pi reads both locations; all agents dedupe by real path.

## Plugins (`moorage.toml` manifest)

A `moorage.toml` at the repo root (or passed directly as `SOURCE`) upgrades a repo to
a plugin. **Its absence changes nothing** — no-manifest repos keep the exact behavior
above.

```
 = "conversate"          # optional plugin label (names placed hook files)
[]                    # optional preferences (see Precedence)
 = "dev"                 # dev | normal | local
 = ["claude", "pi", "omp", "codex"]
[[]]
 = "."                   # payload dir, repo-root-relative ("." = repo root)
 = "normal"              # optional per-skill override
 = ["claude"]       # optional per-skill override
[[]]
 = "hooks/claude/settings-snippet.json"   # merged into <claude-root>/settings.json
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <pi-root>/agent/extensions/
[[]]
 = "hooks/pi/conv-turn-counter.ts"         # placed into <omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/
 = "pre"                                    # default "pre" when omitted
[[]]
 = "hooks/codex/hooks.json"                # merged into <codex-root>/hooks.json
[]
 = ["python scripts/example.py init"]         # optional; cwd = canonical skill dir
```
### Preference precedence

`CLI flags > per-skill entry > [install] table > built-in defaults` (mode `dev`, all
four harnesses). `--mode` / `--harnesses` on the command line mean "override the
manifest". The `harnesses` list gates both the skill links (`claude` → claude-root
link; any of `pi`/`omp`/`codex` → agents-root link) and the hook wiring per harness.
Per-skill `harnesses` gate that skill's links; plugin-level hooks follow
`CLI > [install] > default`.

### Hook FILES (pi, omp)

Placed as **file symlinks** named `moorage-{label}-{basename}` (label = manifest
`name`, else the first skill's name) pointing at the canonical copy inside
`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...` — so dev/normal switching is transparent. If file
symlinks are unavailable (Windows without Developer Mode) the file is **copied** with
a loud warning, and doctor tracks drift of copied placements. Junctions are dir-only
and hardlinks die across volumes, so neither is used for files. Hook scripts must
live inside a `[[skills]]` payload (otherwise no canonical home copy exists — the
install refuses that hook).

### Registration MERGES (claude, codex)

The snippet's `hooks` block merges into the target config via a serde_json
round-trip that preserves unrelated keys:

- claude → `<claude-root>/settings.json`
- codex → `<codex-root>/hooks.json`(plus a printed reminder that codex loads hooks only with`[features] hooks = true`in`~/.codex/config.toml`— moorage**never**edits that file)

Merges are **append-if-absent** (exact-equality dedupe ⇒ idempotent re-installs), and
a syntactically invalid target config is refused, never clobbered. Before the
**first** modification of each config, a `.bak` copy goes into `~/.moorage/backups/`
(named `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`, recorded in state).

**Command-path rewriting** (design ruling; the v2 exact rule is unrecovered): every
whitespace-separated token of a `command` / `commandWindows` string that resolves —
relative to an installed skill payload root — to an existing file is rewritten to the
absolute path of that file under the canonical home
(`~/.moorage/skills/{name}/...`). The **home** path, never the source repo path, so
dev-mode symlinks keep the loop live. Rewritten paths containing spaces are quoted; a
token that itself contains spaces can never match (whitespace split — a known v2
limitation). Snippets should therefore reference their scripts by payload-relative
paths (e.g. `hooks/claude/counter.ps1`).

### Reversibility

Every inserted JSON entry is persisted **verbatim** in `state.toml` *and* is
self-marked by containing the `~/.moorage/skills/{name}` path in its command (no
marker keys are injected — that would fight harness schema validation). `uninstall`:

- unmerges exactly the recorded entries (falling back to the home-path marker for
entries a user edited in place); emptied configs are left as `{}`, never deleted;
- removes placed hook files and agent links (links are dropped, targets untouched);
- removes the home entry — for dev mode the **symlink only**, never the target repo;
- deletes the state record.

Source repositories are never touched. Legacy state records (pre-plugin, five fields)
still load; uninstalling one derives the two conventional agent-link paths and
deletes each **only after verifying it actually points into the moorage home** —
anything else is skipped with a warning.

### post_install

Commands run after all components are placed, with `cwd` = the canonical skill dir in
the home (first skill for multi-skill plugins). Each command is echoed and its
outcome recorded in state. `--no-post-install` skips them (recorded as `skipped`). A
failing command **reports loudly, marks the state record ( failed(N)), sets exit
code 1, and does NOT roll back the install** (design ruling — fix the cause and
re-run, or uninstall).

`update` never runs post_install.## update

- **dev**installs: verify and repair the whole chain — home link, agent links, hook files; re-apply merges when snippets changed (stale recorded entries are unmerged, new ones merged; stale hook files removed).
- **normal**installs: hash-compare (in-crate FNV-1a-64 over the payload tree) and re-copy- **only if the source changed**;- **refuse**when the installed copy was hand-edited (or when a legacy record has no stored hash to verify against) —- `--force`overrides.

## doctor

Read-only, always. Checks: state.toml parse health; full chain integrity (agent link
→ home → payload); dangling/re-targeted links; placed hook files (missing, dangling,
copy drift vs canonical); merged registrations (recorded entries still present,
target configs valid); **orphaned** moorage-marked entries (home path in the command
but absent from state); unmanaged entries (reported, never touched) incl. pi
name-rule violations; shadowing (same name under claude-root and agents-root
resolving to different real paths); normal-mode content drift vs source; dev-mode git
hygiene (dirty tree, non-main branch — best effort); manifest preference drift
(manifest prefers a different mode than installed); `AGENTS.md` inside a skill dir
(pi issue #2473). `--json` emits the findings machine-readably. Exit code is 0 even
with findings; nonzero means doctor itself failed to run.

## Conflicts, idempotency, dry-run

- An entry already resolving to the right target is left alone (idempotent re-runs); merges dedupe by exact equality.
- A conflicting foreign entry is **refused**with a clear message;`--force`renames it to a sibling`{name}.bak-N`and replaces it.
- `--dry-run`prints the full plan and changes nothing (configs are only read).

## Roots (for tests / alternate setups)

Flag > env > default, uniformly:

| Setting | Flag | Env | Default | Used for |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| home | `--home` | `MOORAGE_HOME` | `~/.moorage` | canonical home, state, backups |
| agents root | `--agents-root` | `MOORAGE_AGENTS_ROOT` | `~/.agents` | pi/omp/codex skill links |
| claude root | `--claude-root` | `MOORAGE_CLAUDE_ROOT` | `~/.claude` | Claude skill links + `settings.json`merges |
| pi root | `--pi-root` | `MOORAGE_PI_ROOT` | `~/.pi` | hook files under `agent/extensions/` |
| omp root | `--omp-root` | `MOORAGE_OMP_ROOT` | `~/.omp` | hook files under `hooks/{stage}/` |
| codex root | `--codex-root` | `MOORAGE_CODEX_ROOT` | `~/.codex` | `hooks.json`merges |

## state.toml

`~/.moorage/state.toml` records, per skill: `name`, `mode`, `source`, `installed`/
`updated` (epoch secs), and — for plugin installs — `plugin` label, `manifest` path,
effective `harnesses`, `home_kind` (symlink/junction/copy), `copy_hash` (normal
mode), `[[links]]` (path/kind/target), `[[hook_files]]` (path/kind/target),
`[[merges]]` (file/event/verbatim entry), `[[post_install]]` (command/status), and
`[[backups]]` (original/backup). Legacy five-field records load unchanged.

## Windows link fallback

Directory links try: real symlink (needs Developer Mode or elevation) → NTFS
**junction** via `cmd /c mklink /J` (no privileges) → **copy** with a loud warning.
File placements try: file symlink → copy (drift tracked by doctor). On non-Windows,
symlinks are used directly.

## Unverified upstream paths (honesty notes)

- **omp**: upstream documents only- *project-level*- `.omp/hooks/{stage}/*.ts`discovery. The user-level- `<omp-root>/hooks/{stage}/`placement is a- **best-documented-guess**(unverified upstream). doctor emits a- `warn`note when omp hook files are installed; override with- `--omp-root`.
- **codex**: whether codex reads a- *user-level*- `hooks.json`at all is- **unverified**(only project-level- `.codex/hooks.json`is documented). doctor emits a- `warn`note when codex merges are installed; override with- `--codex-root`.
- **pi**(- `~/.pi/agent/extensions`) and- **claude**(- `~/.claude/settings.json`) are documented/known paths.

## Design rulings (unrecovered v2 details, decided here)

- **Command rewriting token rule**: whitespace token → resolve against installed payload roots (manifest order, first match) → rewrite to the absolute canonical home path; quote only when the result contains spaces; absolute tokens skipped.
- **Mode name**: the CLI keeps- `dev|normal`;- `local`(the v2 name) is accepted as an alias both on the CLI and in manifests.
- **omp**:- `stage`default- `"pre"`(the only value ever observed).
- **post_install failure**: loud warning +- `failed(N)`in state + exit 1, no rollback;- `--no-post-install`records- `skipped`;- `update`never runs post_install.
- `--force`backups- `{name}.bak-N`convention (the pinned minimal-Rust behavior) instead of moving into- `~/.moorage/backups/`; the backups dir holds config- `.bak`snapshots only, named- `{basename}.{epoch}.bak`.
- **backups/ contents are permanent**: uninstall does not delete taken backups (traceability).
- **Multi-skill plugins**: post_install cwd = first skill's canonical dir; hook artifacts are named after the manifest- `name`(else the first skill); the plugin component ledger (hook files, merges, post_install, backups) rides on the first skill's state record.
- **Manifests must declare**: a manifest with no skills entry is an error (hooks need a payload to live in).- `[[skills]]`
- **Corrupt state.toml**: mutating commands refuse to run over an unparseable ledger (protecting the live records); doctor reports it as a- `fail`finding.
- `update`flags- `--force`(attested) plus- `--dry-run`(inferred-carried).
- **Content hashing**: in-crate FNV-1a-64 (stable across releases, zero deps) — std's- `DefaultHasher`is explicitly not used for persisted hashes.

## Build

```
cargo build --release          # binary at target/release/moorage(.exe)
cargo install --path .         # optional: install to ~/.cargo/bin
```
Tests: `cargo test` (unit: manifest parse, merge/unmerge/rewrite, state round-trip
incl. legacy records) and `python -m pytest tests/ -q` (29 black-box tests against
the built binary with all six roots pinned to temp dirs; set `MOORAGE_BIN` to point
at a specific exe, else `target/debug/moorage`).

Requires a stable Rust toolchain. Dependencies: `clap` (CLI), `serde` + `toml`
(manifests + state), `serde_json` (registration merges).

# polkadot_jemalloc_shim - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/polkadot-jemalloc-shim/0.6.0/polkadot_jemalloc_shim/

## Expand description

Shim crate to enable `jemalloc-allocator` feature for Polkadot crates.

Because [there doesn’t exist any easier way right now](https://github.com/rust-lang/cargo/issues/1197), we
need an entire crate to handle `jemalloc` enabling/disabling. This way we can enable it by
default on Linux, but have it optional on all other OSes.

# sim_lib_sound_core - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/sim-lib-sound-core/0.1.0-rc.1/sim_lib_sound_core/

## Expand description

Core sound primitives for the SIM music constellation.

This crate defines the foundational acoustic types shared by the
sound/synthesis layer: [ Frequency](https://docs.rs/struct.Frequency.html),

[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Amplitude.html)

`Amplitude`[quantities; the](https://docs.rs/struct.Phase.html)

`Phase`[,](https://docs.rs/struct.Partial.html)

`Partial`[, and](https://docs.rs/struct.Envelope.html)

`Envelope`[models that build a spectral tone from sinusoidal components; and helpers for default envelopes and equal-temperament pitch-to-frequency conversion.](https://docs.rs/struct.Tone.html)

`Tone`## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Amplitude](https://docs.rs/struct.Amplitude.html)
- A non-negative linear amplitude.
- [Envelope](https://docs.rs/struct.Envelope.html)
- An attack/decay/sustain/release amplitude envelope.
- [Frequency](https://docs.rs/struct.Frequency.html)
- A positive frequency in hertz.
- [Partial](https://docs.rs/struct.Partial.html)
- A single sinusoidal component of a tone.
- [Phase](https://docs.rs/struct.Phase.html)
- A phase angle in radians.
- [Tone](https://docs.rs/struct.Tone.html)
- A complete tone: a set of `Partial``Envelope`

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Envelope](https://docs.rs/enum.EnvelopeShape.html)- Shape
- The interpolation curve applied across an `Envelope`
- [Sound](https://docs.rs/enum.SoundCoreError.html)- Core - Error
- Error raised when sound primitives are constructed with invalid values.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [default_](https://docs.rs/fn.default_envelope.html)- envelope
- Returns a general-purpose default envelope (short attack and decay, high sustain, moderate release, linear shape).
- [equal_](https://docs.rs/fn.equal_temperament_frequency.html)- temperament_ - frequency
- Returns the 12-tone equal-temperament frequency of `pitch`, with A4 (MIDI 69) anchored at 440 Hz.

# vize_fresco - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_fresco/0.273.0/vize_fresco/

## Expand description

Fresco - Vue TUI Framework

A high-performance Terminal User Interface framework for Vue.js, similar to React Ink but built with Rust for performance.

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- **Terminal Control**: Cross-platform terminal handling via crossterm
- **Flexbox Layout**: Layout engine powered by taffy
- **CJK Support**: Full Unicode text handling including Japanese IME
- **Efficient Rendering**: Double-buffered differential rendering

[§](https://docs.rs#architecture)Architecture

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Vue Components                        │
│                  (Box, Text, Input)                       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  Vue Custom Renderer                     │
│                    (TypeScript)                          │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
                          ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                   NAPI Bindings                          │
│             (Rust <-> Node.js bridge)                    │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │
        ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
        ▼                 ▼                 ▼
┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐ ┌───────────────┐
│   Terminal    │ │    Layout     │ │    Render     │
│   (backend,   │ │   (taffy,     │ │   (tree,      │
│    buffer)    │ │    flex)      │ │    diff)      │
└───────────────┘ └───────────────┘ └───────────────┘
        │                                   │
        ▼                                   ▼
┌───────────────┐                 ┌───────────────┐
│     Input     │                 │     Text      │
│  (keyboard,   │                 │   (width,     │
│   mouse, ime) │                 │    segment)   │
└───────────────┘                 └───────────────┘
```
## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use component::`- [InputNode](https://docs.rs/component/struct.InputNode.html);
- `pub use component::`- [TextNode](https://docs.rs/component/struct.TextNode.html);
- `pub use input::`- [Event](https://docs.rs/input/enum.Event.html);
- `pub use input::`- [ImeState](https://docs.rs/input/ime/struct.ImeState.html);
- `pub use input::`- [KeyEvent](https://docs.rs/input/struct.KeyEvent.html);
- `pub use input::`- [MouseEvent](https://docs.rs/input/struct.MouseEvent.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [FlexStyle](https://docs.rs/layout/struct.FlexStyle.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [LayoutEngine](https://docs.rs/layout/struct.LayoutEngine.html);
- `pub use layout::`- [Rect](https://docs.rs/layout/struct.Rect.html);
- `pub use render::`- [RenderNode](https://docs.rs/render/struct.RenderNode.html);
- `pub use render::`- [RenderTree](https://docs.rs/render/struct.RenderTree.html);
- `pub use terminal::`- [Backend](https://docs.rs/terminal/struct.Backend.html);
- `pub use terminal::`- [Buffer](https://docs.rs/terminal/struct.Buffer.html);
- `pub use terminal::`- [Cell](https://docs.rs/terminal/struct.Cell.html);
- `pub use terminal::`- [Cursor](https://docs.rs/terminal/struct.Cursor.html);

# vize_musea - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_musea/0.273.0/vize_musea/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#vize_musea)vize_musea

Musea - Component gallery and documentation for Vize.

[§](https://docs.rs#name-origin)Name Origin

**Musea** (plural of museum) represents a gallery space where art is
displayed and documented. Similarly, `vize_musea` provides a gallery
for Vue components, allowing developers to view and interact with
components in isolation - similar to Storybook.

[§](https://docs.rs#concepts)Concepts

- **Art**: A component variation/state (replaces “story”)
- **Art file**(- `*.art.vue`): File defining arts
- **Gallery**: Display area for arts
- **Palette**: Interactive controls panel

[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

This crate is optimized for high performance:

- **Zero-copy parsing**: All strings are borrowed from source
- **Arena allocation**: Uses- `vize_carton::Bump`for fast allocation
- **Minimal allocations**: Only allocates when absolutely necessary
- **Fast byte-level parsing**: Uses- `memchr`and- `memmem`for O(n) search

[§](https://docs.rs#usage)Usage

```
use vize_carton::Bump;
use vize_musea::{parse_art, transform_to_csf};
use vize_musea::types::ArtParseOptions;
let allocator = Bump::new();
let source = r#"
<script setup lang="ts">
defineArt("./Button.vue", { title: "Button" });
</script>
<art>
  <variant name="Primary" default>
    <Button variant="primary">Click me</Button>
  </variant>
  <variant name="Secondary">
    <Button variant="secondary">Click me</Button>
  </variant>
</art>
"#;
// Parse Art file with arena allocator
let art = parse_art(&allocator, source, ArtParseOptions::default()).unwrap();
// Transform to Storybook CSF
let csf = transform_to_csf(&art);
println!("Generated: {}", csf.filename);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

- Zero-copy parsing of `*.art.vue`files
- Type-safe variant definitions
- Storybook CSF 3.0 export
- Visual Regression Testing (VRT) support
- Interactive props palette

# vize_atelier_sfc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/vize_atelier_sfc/0.273.0/vize_atelier_sfc/

## Expand description

Vue Single File Component (.vue) compiler.

This module provides parsing and compilation of Vue SFCs, following the Vue.js core structure:

- `parse`- SFC parsing into descriptor blocks
- `compile_script`- Script/script setup compilation
- `compile_template`- Template block compilation (DOM and Vapor)
- `compile`- Main SFC compilation orchestration
- `style`- Style block compilation with scoped CSS
- `css`- Low-level CSS compilation with LightningCSS

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
use vize_atelier_sfc::{parse_sfc, compile_sfc, SfcParseOptions, SfcCompileOptions};
let source = r#"
<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'
const count = ref(0)
</script>
<template>
  <button @click="count++">{{ count }}</button>
</template>
"#;
let descriptor = parse_sfc(source, SfcParseOptions::default()).unwrap();
let result = compile_sfc(&descriptor, SfcCompileOptions::default()).unwrap();
println!("{}", result.code);
```
